text:
St. Therese criticized exaggerations about Mary in a refreshing passage:

"I'd first make people understand how little is known by us about her life.

"We shouldn't say unlikely things or things we don't know anything about! For example, that when she was very little, at the age of three, the Blessed Virgin went up to the Temple to offer herself to God, burning with sentiments of love and extraordinary fervor. While perhaps she went there very simply out of obedience to her parents.

"Again, why say, with reference to the aged Simeon's prophetic words, that the Blessed Virgin had the Passion of Jesus constantly before her mind from that moment onward? 'And a sword will pierce through your soul also,' the old man said, It wasn't for the present, you see, little Mother, it was a general prediction for the future.

"For a sermon on the Blessed Virgin to please me and do me any good, I must see her real life, not her imagined life. I'm sure that her real life was very simple. They show her to us as unapproachable, but they should present her as imitable, bringing out her virtues, saying that she lived by faith just like ourselves, giving proofs of this from the gospel, where we read: 'And they did not understand the words which He spoke to them. ' And that other no less mysterious statement: 'His father and mother marveled at what was said about Him.' This admiration presupposes a certain surprise, don't you think so, little Mother?

"We know very well that the Blessed Virgin is Queen of heaven and earth, but she is more mother than queen; and we should not say, on account of her prerogatives, that she surpasses all the saints in glory just as the sun at its rising makes the stars disappear from sight. My God! How strange that would be! A mother who makes her children's glory vanish! I myself think just the contrary. I believe she'll increase the splendor of the elect very much.

"It's good to speak about her prerogatives, but we should not stop at this, and if, in a sermon, we are obliged from beginning to end to exclaim and say: Ah! Ah!, we would grow tired! Who knows whether some soul would not reach the point of feeling a certain estrangement from a creature so superior and would not say: 'If things are such, it's better to go and shine as well as one is able in some little corner!'" (Her Last Conversations)

Prince and a group of military contractors pitched Trump advisers a $25 billion proposal to remove up to 12 million people. The plan includes processing camps on military bases, a fleet of roughly 100 private planes, and thousands of trained private personnel authorized to make arrests.

Prince has argued the federal government cannot scale ICE and CBP fast enough on its own to hit the administration’s targets and that private logistics and manpower will be required.

The proposal has circulated among White House officials. Whether it is adopted remains to be seen, but the offer shows how far some are willing to go to expand the deportation operation beyond current government capacity.

text:
The Surprising Mathematical Truth Behind the Midterm Election Disaster🔥

I must ensure that I don’t repeat the same mistakes this time around. Take the liberal media outlet Vox, for instance; they asked me something to the effect of, "How do you know your previous judgment was wrong?" I replied, "Look, everyone does this. Everyone claims they dislike having their own ideology challenged."

Consider the amendments—passed overwhelmingly in states like Colorado and Washington, both of which lean Democratic—that prohibit biological males from entering women’s spaces or participating in women’s sports. Could you find 100 members—or even 50% to 52%—of the current Democratic-controlled Congress who would sign off on such a bill? Could you find even 50 members who would acknowledge that there are, in fact, only two biological sexes? The answer is no. Remember, the electorate—those who actually vote—tends to be far more extreme than the general public. They live in fear of the political class and its judgment, leading them to ignore self-evident truths that most Americans accept. Therefore, the only way to challenge ourselves and arrive at better answers is to examine the data.

Advertisement
To begin with, looking at the popular vote, the Democrats appeared to be leading by 13 percentage points—a margin near historic highs for a House popular vote. It was on par with the Watergate era—an enormous lead. We don’t have the final, precise figures yet, as California won’t finish counting its ballots until the next election cycle is already underway. Once they finally finalize their results, we’ll likely be heading into the next election. Yet, in 2024, the popular vote shifted to a 2-point lead for the Republicans. That represents a swing of roughly 15 percentage points—a total shift of 15 points. This is based on estimates from *The New York Times*, whose polling has proven to be highly accurate.

According to the polling data, the two demographic groups that showed the most dramatic shift in their stance toward the Republican Party were young people and Latinos. Support among young people has shifted 33 percentage points toward the Democratic Party; among Latinos, support has shifted 29 percentage points toward the Democrats. Of course, these two groups are not entirely distinct—many young people are also Latino. Consequently, a shift in the stance of one group often reflects a shift in the other, as there is significant overlap between them.

Two points are worth noting here: younger Latinos tend to lean further to the left than older Latinos. Similarly, Latinos with an annual income of $50,000 or less are more likely to lean left than those with higher incomes (such as $100,000 or $200,000). This influences both their political alignment and their likelihood of turning out to vote. This suggests two separate dynamics: the Democratic Party has succeeded in both persuading more Latinos to adopt their policy positions and mobilizing more of those supporters to cast their ballots—both of which contribute to the observed shift in the Latino electorate toward the Democrats. Florida is a particularly useful case study: it offers a wealth of data, a large Latino population, and—unlike Texas—it registers voters by party affiliation. (Incidentally, this is something I intend to advocate for the rest of my life: getting every state to register voters by party, as it would vastly simplify data analysis.)

Unlike other states that register voters by party—such as Arizona and New York, both of which also have large Latino populations—Florida actually manages to count all its ballots on election night. Can you imagine? Wouldn't it be wonderful if New York (where counting is still ongoing) and Arizona (also still counting) could likewise finish tallying all their votes on election night? That would be fantastic!

🚩The affordability poll mantra helped Democrats triumph

(Sensible Article which states that the Democratic landslide was downstream of two events: Zohran Mamdani's election as mayor of New York City and Donald Trump's maniacal decision to go to war with Iran.Mamdani's greatest service to his country was to meet Trump and allow the two of them to be captured in a single frame. The juxtaposition of age and youth, decadence and renewal, corruption and rectitude, insularity and cosmo politanism, bigotry and idealism doesn't explain what happened in these elections but it does illustrate the choices that were on offer. Mamdani wasn't running for election but like a grinning ghost, he was on the ticket )

Mamdani's campaign set out the material pitch for Democrats across the country in a single word: affordability. He produced a mantra that drove that one-word message home: fast and free buses, universal childcare and a rent freeze. Abdul El-Sayed's three-part version of affordability was both different and the same: money out of politics, money in your pockets, Medicare for all. The more Centrist candidates like Jon Ossoff, Annie Andrews, James Talarico and Scott Colom produced their own variations on the affordability theme. Ossoff argued that Republican corruption inflated the prices of drugs and housing, Talarico watered down free childcare to address Texan sensibilities but promised tax credits to help parents out while Andrews and Colom promised to cap utility rates and transport costs.

Professional moderates, nervous about avowed progressives making the political weather, have argued that a materialist pitch is not new. In the context of American politics in the time of Trump, it absolutely is. Where demoralised establishment Democrats like Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries hyperventilated to no effect about Trump's authoritar-ianism and corruption, Mamdani's successful insistence that the State could and should intervene to im prove the material lives of working people was a precedent, a unified mes sage and, politically, a game-changer.

Ironically, when Mamdani won the mayoralty, both Republican oper atives and Cuomo Democrats warned that New Yorkers had handed Trump a socialist bogeyman to vilify in the mid-terms. After the landslide, the best these triangulating Centrists could do was argue that the Sun Belt wins in Texas, Georgia, the Carolinas and, possibly, Mississippi were a triumph for moderation, not the re-lentless focus on affordability that Mamdani pioneered and pulled off. It's a simple rhetorical trick: when Democrats win, Centrists claim the electorate has moved Left to the Centre and when Democrats lose, these same ideologues argue that Leftist excess has pushed the elector ate Right, past the Centre.

Mamdani's second achievement was to free Democratic politics of a moral liability that had stifled its progressive instincts and warped its

commitment to liberal principles. Despite the vaunted polarisation of US politics and the breakdown of cooperation across the aisle, the issue that joined Republicans and Democrats into a grotesque uniparty was their lockstep support for Israel and its unending violence in Gaza and the West Bank. The party's deference to the American Israeli Public Affairs Committee (its leaders in Congress are AIPAC clients) meant that the only sanctioned form of mainstream liberalism was liberal Zionism exem plified by Joe Biden's performative embrace of Benjamin Netanyahu.

Mamdani called time on this all fours 'liberalism' during the prima ry debate when he refused to join the other candidates in chorusing their determination to pledge fealty by making Israel their first port of call after the election. Mamdani said he would stay home in the five bor oughs of New York and tend to his constituents. In the most Jewish city in America, he touched that third rail and didn't fizzle. In one move, he de-Zionised the election. By calling the war in Gaza a genocide, he gave voice to Democrats, especially young people who had been horrified by the slaughter on their screens. Israel's

methodical killing in Gaza was the principal cause for the massive shift in public opinion away from Israel but it was Mamdani who made a rejec tion of America's complicity in this slaughter electorally sayable.

In retrospect, the ways in which Zionism deranged US public life will become clearer but we can see in the aftermath of the mid-terms the ex-tent of the fever that broke. The slan-dering of Mamdani and El-Sayed as antisemites, the routine eruptions of the Anti-Defamation League, the al most-comical determination of Bari Weiss's Free Press and The Atlantic's stable of hasbarist writers to smear Israel's critics and the systematic bid by Trump's tame tycoons like Bill Ackman, Larry Ellison and Jeff Bezos to make genuflection to Israel a litmus test for permissible speech will seem McCarthyesque to the historian of this moment. But the most vivid illus-tration of the change that Mamdani catalysed was the bizarre self-de-struction of the Congresswoman, Haley Stevens, El-Sayed's principal primary opponent.

Haley Stevens became infamous for a befuddling speech in which she declared that "Israel comes to me in my dreams." Her unhinged fervour,

and the all-round weirdness of her demeanour, should have been dis-qualifying but she was handpicked by Chuck Schumer as the preferred can-didate of the Democratic establish-ment. The only reason she was chosen over the others was that her zeal for Israel guaranteed that AIPAC would spend a mountain of money to get her elected. This would, as a bonus, ensure that the hugely credentialled but uncompromisingly anti-Zionist, El-Sayed, lost. That didn't happen, but that was the plan and if it hadn't been for El-Sayed's pugnacity and Mamdani's precedent, it might have worked. In the end, the Democratic establishment's chosen candidate en-dorsed El-Sayed's Republican oppo-nent. It was the perfect example of the Zionist obliviousness that had mud-dled Democratic politics for decades.

DENO NEW YOR

But none of this might have hap-pened if the United States of America didn't have in Trump a mad emper-or determined to create a Bellum Americanum, a world disordered by war. Indians know that terrible gov-ernment policies like demonetisation that cause widespread distress don't necessarily lead to electoral defeat. It's possible that Trump's whimsicall tariff policy could have been sold as a defence of America and an asser-tion of American hegemony. But America's war with Iran, with its atrocities, its casualties, its emptying of the US arsenal, its closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and the inexorable rise in the price of fuel made two sepa-rate parts of Mamdani's narrative co-here and resonate with the American electorate on the eve of the mid-term vote.

Never had American well-be-ing been in greater conflict with America's extravagant military spon-sorship of Israel and its wars. At a time of inflation and hardship, the US was bleeding money, men and materi-el on a war with no end in sight. When El-Sayed argued "[i]t shouldn't be this hard to pay your taxes and know that that money is going to be spent on you and your kids rather than dropping bombs on somebody else and their kids", affordability and the moral in-dictment of the killing of Palestinian and Iranian children became a single argument.

Mamdani's greatest service to his country was to meet Trump and allow the two of them to be captured in a single frame. The juxtaposition of age and youth, decadence and renewal, corruption and rectitude, insularity and cosmopolitanism, bigotry and idealism doesn't explain what happened in these elections but it does illustrate the choices that were on offer. Mamdani wasn't running for election but like a grinning ghost, he was on the ticket.

Arabica coffee futures traded around $3.1 per pound, a level not seen since March, as traders weighed signs of tightening inventories while monitoring the pace of Brazil's harvest. Arabica certified stocks at ICE fell by another 3,069 bags to 377,465, the lowest level since March 2024. The market also factored in delays to Brazil’s harvest due to rainfall in major producing areas, alongside quality concerns, with investment funds increasing activity amid weather uncertainties. Coffee harvest in Brazil reached 44% as of June 24, below 51% a year earlier and the five-year average of 47%, according to Safras & Mercado. Brazilian coffee, beef and tropical fruit will still be tariffed 40%, says Brazil’s vice president

RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazilian Vice President Geraldo Alckmin said Saturday that Brazilian exported goods to the U.S. including coffee, beef and tropical fruits would still be tariffed 40%, despite President Donald Trump’s decision to remove some import taxes.

In a dramatic move on Friday, Trump scrapped levies announced in April on what he called ‘Liberation Day’ in hopes of encouraging domestic production and lifting the U.S. economy. Brazil at the time was hit with a 10% tariff.

But in July, Trump imposed a further 40% tariff, citing — among other reasons — the trial of his ally, former President Jair Bolsonaro, which he called a “witch hunt.” Proceedings went ahead regardless and in September Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison for attempting a coup.

Alckmin said some products, such as orange juice, would now have a zero tariff as they were not targeted by the additional 40%. But that extra tariff remains in place on products including coffee, beef and tropical fruits, such as mangos and pineapples.

While Brazil’s vice president welcomed Trump’s latest decision, which he called “positive” and a “step in the right direction,” he said there remained a “distortion that needs to be corrected.”

“Everyone got 10% less, but in Brazil’s case, which had 50%, we ended up with 40%, which is very high,” Alckmin told journalists in the capital Brasilia.

Alckmin said that Friday's decision means that 26% of Brazilian goods are now entering the U.S. without additional tariffs. That's up from 23%.

Trump’s July decision, which was overtly political as Brazil has a trade deficit with the United States, led to the worst U.S.-Brazil relations in history.

Those relations have since improved, and in October Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Trump met in Malaysia.

“President Lula’s conversation with President Donald Trump was important in terms of dialogue and negotiation,” Alckmin said on Saturday.

After that encounter, Lula said he was confident the two countries would soon reach a trade deal.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Brazil’s Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira met for 50 minutes this week to further the conversation.

The Trump administration has insisted that its tariffs helped fill government coffers and weren’t a major factor in higher prices at grocery stores around the country. But Democrats were quick to paint Friday’s move as an acknowledgment that Trump’s policies were hurting American pocketbooks.

Record-high beef prices have been a particular concern, and Trump had said he intended to take action to try and lower them. Trump’s tariffs on Brazil, a major beef exporter, had been a factor.

Back in Brazil, the Brazilian Association of the Coffee Industry said it would continue to monitor the situation.

“(We) will keep working to ensure legal certainty, competitiveness, and predictability for the Brazilian coffee industry,” the group’s president, Pavel Cardoso, said in a statement. (Wires, A.I News)

text:
JUST IN: Diversified restaurant brands lift stocks, while single‑brand chains fall.

Restaurant stocks split sharply this year, with multi‑brand groups posting gains while single‑brand chains have slipped. Brinker International, Darden Restaurants and Restaurant Brands International are up roughly 32%, 18% and 12% year‑to‑date, respectively. Those companies own chains ranging from Chili’s to Olive Garden, LongHorn Steakhouse, Burger King and Tim Hortons.

In contrast, McDonald’s, Chipotle, Cava, Wendy’s, Shake Shack and Domino’s have all dropped this year, with several down double‑digit percentages. Those companies all have one core chain to their names.

Analysts say the performance gap highlights the benefits of a diversified restaurant business, especially when any misstep can push cash‑strapped consumers elsewhere.

Investors will get another look at how operating multiple chains—or not—affects performance when major restaurant companies report quarterly results starting next week. One company that could be watching is Inspire Brands, the owner of Dunkin’, Buffalo Wild Wings and Jimmy John’s, which is moving toward going public.

“A business built around one main restaurant concept depends more heavily on that brand holding consumers’ attention,” said Nick Setyan, a restaurant analyst at Mizuho Securities. “Whereas a company with a portfolio has other potential sources of sales if one brand loses momentum.”

Setyan noted that the dynamic has played out between Darden’s key brands. In the latest reported quarter, LongHorn’s comparable sales rose 6.2% compared with Olive Garden’s 1.1%. LongHorn’s growth has outpaced Olive Garden’s for months.

KeyBanc Capital Markets also cited Darden’s portfolio as a positive in an October research note, saying it gives the company “exposure to a broad range of consumers.” The firm has a buy‑equivalent rating on Darden and a $237 price target, compared with a price of around $215 as of Thursday.

Restaurant Brands International offers exposure to different categories and markets through Burger King, Tim Hortons and Popeyes. But its portfolio does not fully insulate the company from a weak brand.

In the second quarter, Burger King’s U.S. comparable sales accelerated to 8.5%, from 5.8% in the first quarter, while Tim Hortons’ Canadian comparable sales slowed to just 0.1%, from 1.5% over the same period. That left Burger King’s turnaround carrying more of the portfolio as Tim Hortons stalled.

Setyan said Burger King’s recent strong performance has been central to the company’s momentum, helped by its ability to better communicate its value items to customers as McDonald’s sales growth slowed. “If it weren’t for Burger King’s current performance, I don’t know if Restaurant Brands would be going so well,” he said.

Mizuho initiated coverage of Restaurant Brands on Oct. 20 with a buy‑equivalent rating and an $85 price target. Shares traded at about $76 as of Thursday.

A focus on one brand can also be a strength. Starbucks and Cheesecake Factory have been restaurant‑stock standouts this year, showing how a clear brand identity and investment can drive outperformance when execution and customer demand click. Their shares have climbed 21% and nearly 123%, respectively, this year.

Starbucks, for its part, said it would not buy Chipotle after reportedly considering a massive buyout that would have diversified its business.

As the industry heads into the next quarter, investors will watch whether the diversified approach continues to pay off or whether the focus on a single brand can still deliver superior returns.

Brazilian coffee, beef and tropical fruit will still be tariffed 40%, says Brazil’s vice president

RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazilian Vice President Geraldo Alckmin said Saturday that Brazilian exported goods to the U.S. including coffee, beef and tropical fruits would still be tariffed 40%, despite President Donald Trump’s decision to remove some import taxes.

In a dramatic move on Friday, Trump scrapped levies announced in April on what he called ‘Liberation Day’ in hopes of encouraging domestic production and lifting the U.S. economy. Brazil at the time was hit with a 10% tariff.

But in July, Trump imposed a further 40% tariff, citing — among other reasons — the trial of his ally, former President Jair Bolsonaro, which he called a “witch hunt.” Proceedings went ahead regardless and in September Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison for attempting a coup.

Alckmin said some products, such as orange juice, would now have a zero tariff as they were not targeted by the additional 40%. But that extra tariff remains in place on products including coffee, beef and tropical fruits, such as mangos and pineapples.

While Brazil’s vice president welcomed Trump’s latest decision, which he called “positive” and a “step in the right direction,” he said there remained a “distortion that needs to be corrected.”

“Everyone got 10% less, but in Brazil’s case, which had 50%, we ended up with 40%, which is very high,” Alckmin told journalists in the capital Brasilia.

Alckmin said that Friday's decision means that 26% of Brazilian goods are now entering the U.S. without additional tariffs. That's up from 23%.

Trump’s July decision, which was overtly political as Brazil has a trade deficit with the United States, led to the worst U.S.-Brazil relations in history.

Those relations have since improved, and in October Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Trump met in Malaysia.

“President Lula’s conversation with President Donald Trump was important in terms of dialogue and negotiation,” Alckmin said on Saturday.

After that encounter, Lula said he was confident the two countries would soon reach a trade deal.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Brazil’s Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira met for 50 minutes this week to further the conversation.

The Trump administration has insisted that its tariffs helped fill government coffers and weren’t a major factor in higher prices at grocery stores around the country. But Democrats were quick to paint Friday’s move as an acknowledgment that Trump’s policies were hurting American pocketbooks.

Record-high beef prices have been a particular concern, and Trump had said he intended to take action to try and lower them. Trump’s tariffs on Brazil, a major beef exporter, had been a factor.

Back in Brazil, the Brazilian Association of the Coffee Industry said it would continue to monitor the situation.

“(We) will keep working to ensure legal certainty, competitiveness, and predictability for the Brazilian coffee industry,” the group’s president, Pavel Cardoso, said in a statement. (Wires, A.I News)

Brazilian coffee, beef and tropical fruit will still be tariffed 40%, says Brazil’s vice president

RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazilian Vice President Geraldo Alckmin said Saturday that Brazilian exported goods to the U.S. including coffee, beef and tropical fruits would still be tariffed 40%, despite President Donald Trump’s decision to remove some import taxes.

In a dramatic move on Friday, Trump scrapped levies announced in April on what he called ‘Liberation Day’ in hopes of encouraging domestic production and lifting the U.S. economy. Brazil at the time was hit with a 10% tariff.

But in July, Trump imposed a further 40% tariff, citing — among other reasons — the trial of his ally, former President Jair Bolsonaro, which he called a “witch hunt.” Proceedings went ahead regardless and in September Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison for attempting a coup.

Alckmin said some products, such as orange juice, would now have a zero tariff as they were not targeted by the additional 40%. But that extra tariff remains in place on products including coffee, beef and tropical fruits, such as mangos and pineapples.

While Brazil’s vice president welcomed Trump’s latest decision, which he called “positive” and a “step in the right direction,” he said there remained a “distortion that needs to be corrected.”

“Everyone got 10% less, but in Brazil’s case, which had 50%, we ended up with 40%, which is very high,” Alckmin told journalists in the capital Brasilia.

Alckmin said that Friday's decision means that 26% of Brazilian goods are now entering the U.S. without additional tariffs. That's up from 23%.

Trump’s July decision, which was overtly political as Brazil has a trade deficit with the United States, led to the worst U.S.-Brazil relations in history.

Those relations have since improved, and in October Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Trump met in Malaysia.

“President Lula’s conversation with President Donald Trump was important in terms of dialogue and negotiation,” Alckmin said on Saturday.

After that encounter, Lula said he was confident the two countries would soon reach a trade deal.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Brazil’s Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira met for 50 minutes this week to further the conversation.

The Trump administration has insisted that its tariffs helped fill government coffers and weren’t a major factor in higher prices at grocery stores around the country. But Democrats were quick to paint Friday’s move as an acknowledgment that Trump’s policies were hurting American pocketbooks.

Record-high beef prices have been a particular concern, and Trump had said he intended to take action to try and lower them. Trump’s tariffs on Brazil, a major beef exporter, had been a factor.

Back in Brazil, the Brazilian Association of the Coffee Industry said it would continue to monitor the situation.

“(We) will keep working to ensure legal certainty, competitiveness, and predictability for the Brazilian coffee industry,” the group’s president, Pavel Cardoso, said in a statement. (Wires, A.I News)

Bill Gates, through the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, invested more than $200 million to develop, promote, and support adoption of the Common Core State Standards. A factual conclusion from the available evidence is:

Bill Gates had extraordinary influence on American education policy through Common Core.

Did Educational Standards Fall Because of Common Core?

This is where the evidence becomes much more complicated.

What the Research Found

Several major studies found that Common Core either produced:

small positive effects in mathematics,
little measurable effect in reading,
mixed results overall.

For example:

A 2020/2021 study comparing early and late Common Core implementation found:

positive effects on 4th- and 8th-grade math scores,
no significant effects on reading scores.

Another implementation study in Chicago found:

improvements in math grades,
higher pass rates,
improved test scores where implementation and teacher training were strong.
Evidence Against Common Core's Effectiveness

Some researchers reached much less favorable conclusions.

Brookings researcher Tom Loveless argued that:

no convincing evidence exists that Common Core significantly improved student achievement.

Education Next summarized research finding:

little overall improvement,
some negative achievement effects on NAEP measures,
failure to achieve many promised gains.

Other analyses concluded that merely raising standards does not automatically improve academic performance.

Did Common Core Cause the Decline in U.S. Educational Performance?

The available evidence does not demonstrate that.

Educational achievement trends are influenced by many factors:

family environment,
teacher quality,
curriculum materials,
demographic changes,
school funding,
technology and social media,
COVID-era learning losses,
state-level implementation differences.

RAND notes that achievement changes cannot easily be attributed solely to Common Core because many other factors affect outcomes simultaneously.

RAND also states that among school-related factors, teacher effectiveness has a larger effect on achievement than standards documents themselves.

Bottom line

The factual record shows that Bill Gates was one of the most influential private actors in modern U.S. education reform, primarily through Common Core funding and advocacy.

However, the claim that Gates' involvement directly caused a measurable decline in educational standards is not supported by a scholarly consensus. The research literature is mixed, with findings ranging from small positive effects in mathematics to little or no overall achievement improvement, and some studies reporting disappointing or negative outcomes relative to expectations.

text:
Vimag Labs Looks to Go Global With Rare-Earth-Free Motor Tech: Targets ₹100 Crore Revenue by FY28 as It Moves Into Commercial Deployment and Scales Up Manufacturing

Core Theme 
Vimag Labs is betting that software-defined, rare-earth-free motors can offer a supply-chain-safe alternative to magnet-based designs, using its Haryana plant and a ₹100-crore FY28 revenue target to push into mobility, industrial, defence and international markets.

The Company and Its Target
Vimag Labs, an advanced motor-technology company developing electric motors without rare-earth permanent magnets, is targeting revenue of ₹100 crore in the next financial year, as it moves into commercial deployment and scales up manufacturing

Manish Seth, CEO and cofounder: “We are currently in deployment mode, and our revenue target is ₹100 crore for the 2027-28 financial year (FY28)”

The firm has set up its first manufacturing facility at MET City in Jhajjar, Haryana

It is preparing to expand its presence across electric mobility, industrial equipment, commercial vehicles and defence and aerospace

The Technology: VMSM Platform
Vimag plans to commercialise its patented Virtual Magnet Synchronous Motor (VMSM) technology across multiple power segments and expand into international markets over the next few years

Seth: the patented platform replaces physical permanent magnets with electronically controlled, software-defined magnetic fields

This eliminates the requirement for rare-earth permanent magnets while delivering comparable or superior performance in efficiency, power density and overall motor performance

Why It Matters
The technology addresses a significant vulnerability in the global electric motor supply chain, given the geographical concentration of rare-earth resources and processing capabilities, and price volatility

Development of alternative motor technologies is significant as India is set to expand its electric vehicle ecosystem, strengthen domestic defence manufacturing and build capabilities in advanced industrial technologies

🚨Russia may have reached the limit of its "peacetime" ability to project force in the Baltic Sea, with the maritime situation "tense" but "stable", the head of Finland's navy has said.

Rear Admiral Tuomas Tiilikainen was speaking to Sky News as a team of US Marines briefly joined a NATO mission tasked with detecting and deterring hostile Russian activity in the area.

This includes attempts by sanctioned Russia-linked shadow fleet vessels to damage or spy on vital underwater data cables, power lines and other critical infrastructure.

"They [the Russian navy] monitor what we do, what NATO does, and we obviously need to monitor and maintain a vigilant guard on what they do and their activities," the Finnish naval chief said in an interview.

"But at the moment, I need to stress, even though the situation at sea is tense, it's still stable and there is no need for us to escalate the situation any further - rather de-escalate."

Rear Admiral Tiilikainen, speaking outside his naval base in Turku, a city on Finland's southwest coast, offered two possible reasons as to why the situation was stable.

"They [the Russians] see that there is no immediate need to ramp up their presence or their readiness in the region, but also maybe they have reached the limits of their capability in peacetime as they like to see here in the Baltic Sea," he said.

text:
Illegal Monday

An Open Letter from the People Who Are Not Interested in Citizenship

Dear Americans,

You keep asking why so many of us undocumented never file for citizenship. You treat it like a mystery or like we do not know better.

We know. You do not.

Illegal just works better.

We get the jobs your own people are locked out of, and it is more pay once you add the benefits your sanctuary zones hand us. We get cash. No payroll tax. We declare a dozen dependents on a stolen Social Security number. No I-9 that survives a real audit. Employers know the arrangement and some of them set it up. They hire us because we will take the number they offer and we will not complain when the hours change or the tools are missing. They show us how it works. The boss pays $12 an hour in the field. We apply for another $25 an hour in tax-paid benefits. Now who is ignorant?

You wanted a living wage and benefits. We took the req that was left after you said no and figured out how to stack benefits until it pays more than you would ever get. See that new truck I drive. Paid it off in cash. You should see the vacation house back where I came from.

Sanctuary states hand out licenses, housing allowance, energy assistance, in-state tuition, and medical care you are told to pay for. We use them. You pay. That is not a loophole we discovered. It is the policy your politicians wrote and then called compassion while cashing checks from the Chamber of Commerce.

We can leave when the work dries up or the heat gets too close and go home rich for a while. Citizenship closes that door. It means taxes, permanent presence, and the same rules that apply to you. Why would we trade a system that pays us to stay illegal for one that charges us to stay legal?

You assumed high-trust people want to join the club. We treat the club as a temporary resource. The work is here. The benefits are here. The enforcement is not. That is not an accident. That is the deal your employers and your elected officials kept in place because it was cheaper than hiring you while you pay the taxes that support us.

A temporary frozen PERM or a speech about the border does not change the math for us. The cash job is still open. The school is still open. The hospital is still open. You get the press release and feel better. Nothing changed for us.

If you want this to stop, stop assuming we are waiting for a form. Most of us are not. We already have what we came for.

A person who is still here because illegal is still working, and people are asking who will pick the lettuce when we make more in cash and benefits than a lot of you make in your tech job.

(Screwtape letter style)

text:
Cities Church in Minnesota releases a statement after Don Lemon and an angry mob of left-wing agitators stormed their church.

"Jesus is real. When we gather on Sunday mornings to worship him, we are gladly giving ourselves to what is most central and sacred in our life together. “We worship Jesus” stretches as the main banner of our church, alongside two other pursuits that flow from it: loving one another and seeking the good of the Twin Cities.

On Sunday, January 18, a group of agitators jarringly disrupted our worship gathering. They accosted members of our congregation, frightened children, and created a scene marked by intimidation and threat. Such conduct is shameful, unlawful, and will not be tolerated. Invading a church service to disrupt the worship of Jesus — or any other act of worship — is protected by neither the Christian Scriptures nor the laws of this nation.

We welcome respectful dialogue about present issues, and about how the realness of Jesus, as revealed in the Bible, provides the only final answers to the world’s most complex and intractable problems.

Jesus Christ, the divine Son of God, lived, died, and rose again for the rescue of all who put their faith in him. He offers a love that transcends cultures, borders, policies, and politics. As those who have been loved and rescued by him, we will not shrink from worshiping Jesus, nor will we stop “teaching and proclaiming the good news that Jesus is the Messiah” (Acts 5:42). Church buildings are meant to be places of peace and solace, where worshipers can hear and live out this message. We therefore call on local, state, and national leaders to protect this fundamental right. We are evaluating next steps with our legal counsel.

– the Elders of Cities Church."

text:
why i preordered @temple , even after the doctors called it a scam

temple is built for a very specific person and i’m that person, 

someone who:

- takes health seriously but runs a chaotic schedule
- already runs a personal health data system
- spends half his life in rooms where privacy matters
- thinks like an early adopter, not a consumer

so i preordered temple batch 01 the night i got an exclusive invite

then watching timeline catches fire, doctors calling it “desi theranos.” @deepigoyal  writing open letters, then apologising. 

half of x calling it a scam, the other half calling it india’s hardware moment.

i read all of it, and decided to keep my preorder, 

here’s the full reasoning, point by point

1. chaotic schedule: health dies in the gaps

2026 was a wake-up call, not going into details, but health went from “i’ll deal with it later” to the main quest, fast.

what i learned - the hard part isn’t knowing what to do. it’s doing it every single day without slipping.

meds on time, meals on time, sleep on time, noticing when something feels off and actually writing it down. none of it is complicated, and all of it breaks when life gets busy.

and my life is always busy, calls across timezones, events, travel, back-to-back meetings.

the problem is friction, every health app lives on my phone, and my phone is a war zone: telegram, x, discord, price alerts. 

a med reminder pops up and it’s competing with a token launch, guess who wins.

temple’s bet is less interface, a buzz on your head can’t be scrolled past, double-tap and speak to log something, with no unlock, no app and no context switch. the best health habit is the one that needs zero willpower.

2. personal health data system: temple is the missing input layer

for months i’ve done the nerd version of health, every lab report goes into structured data, i cross-check providers (found real errors), i’m building my own android app to track meds, meals, symptoms and labs in one place.

the bottleneck was always capture, the data that matters most, like “felt dizzy at 3pm,” “ate late again” or “slept badly,” never gets logged because typing it is annoying.

temple fills exactly that hole, it’s not replacing my stack. it’s feeding it.

3. privacy-heavy rooms -  no mic means it can’t hear the room

every “ai companion” device has a mic, and a mic hears everyone - your cofounder, the person across the table, the deal you’re negotiating, in BD, that’s a non-starter. nobody speaks openly with a recorder in the room.

temple says it has no mic, it reads your voice through vibration, so it can’t hear the room, that’s not a policy you have to trust. 

it’s a hardware constraint.

same logic as self-custody: don’t trust, verify. 

build it so being bad isn’t possible, instead of promising you won’t be, temple also says your conversations are end-to-end encrypted, so not even their team can read them.

it’s the only ai device i’ve seen that respects the people around me, not just me.

4. early adopter: eyes open on the science

let’s be honest, because hype is cheap, the doctors aren’t wrong:

- brainflow isn’t proven to measure the brain. the sensor sits over an artery outside the skull, and the scalp-vs-brain question is still open.
- entropy has zero published validation.
- the hr accuracy claim is internal, not independent.
- the evidence is two small, company-funded preprints, not yet peer reviewed. a start, not proof.
- at ₹85k, it’s 2.5–4× a whoop, oura or apple watch.

the critics should keep pushing, that’s how science is supposed to work.

but i’m not buying temple for brainflow, i’m buying the capture layer: reminders that land, voice logging, sleep data my wrist can’t see.

the brain stuff is a free option, if it validates, great

if it doesn’t, i still got what i paid for.

my rule - trends, not decision

temple helps me spot patterns and stay consistent.
the real calls stay with my doctors and proper diagnostics.

deepinder calls temple “a project, not a product.” 

critics read that as a hedge, i read it as honest. 

in crypto we join protocols early because we believe in the direction, not because v1 is perfect, temple offers the same deal, with a refund button, which is more than most protocols ever gave me.

5. the 14-day test

this isn’t blind faith, there’s a 14-day no-questions return window and refunds anytime before shipping.

when it lands in early 2027, it gets two weeks to earn its place:

- do the reminders fire reliably, every single time?
- does voice logging work on the move and in noisy rooms?
- is the sleep data consistent night to night?
- can i export my own data?

pass, and it stays. fail, and it goes back.

 my data is the judge, 

not the founder and not the doctors.

i’m exactly who temple is for.

founders should ship ambitious things, doctors should demand proof. 

both can be true.

text:
When the Air We Breathe Becomes Toxic: It's Pondicherry's Turn Now

On the eve of Diwali, I came across some deeply shocking air quality readings from Pondicherry. At one point, the city reportedly featured among the world's most polluted locations (one website briefly ranked it as the second most polluted city in the world), with an AQI crossing 1,000 on a live air quality tracker.

Thankfully, the situation improved considerably later in the night, with strong winds from the Bay of Bengal and a brief spell of rain helping disperse the pollutants. But the shock, the psychological distress and the accompanying grief have stayed on in my mind.

When I moved from Delhi to Pondicherry in 2017, there were several reasons behind my decision. The foremost was my proximity to Sri Aurobindo Ashram. The second was the peaceful atmosphere of the city and its relatively grounded, uncomplicated way of life. And the third was something that we often take for granted until we begin to lose it — clean air and a relatively unpolluted environment.

Coming from Delhi, the difference was palpable. The sea breeze (my apartment is close to the beach, and from the terrace I can see the majestic Bay of Bengal), the open skies, the trees and the relatively cleaner air contributed to a quality of life that I deeply valued. It is so unfortunate that even a place like Pondicherry, which has historically offered a relatively healthier environment, is now experiencing such episodes of severe air pollution.

As human beings, we seem to have normalized the gradual destruction of the natural world around us. We celebrate economic growth, urbanization, GDP numbers and technological progress, but often fail to ask a fundamental question: What is the point of development if the very environment that sustains human life becomes increasingly uninhabitable?

Pondicherry deserves better. And so does the planet.
Wake up, humanity!

#Pondicherry #AirPollution #EnvironmentalCrisis #ClimateChange #CleanAir

— Pulkit Sharma
Clinical Psychologist | Psychoanalytic Therapist | Spiritual Counselor & Author
Pondicherry, India

text:
Dig Into Opportunity: Why Working in Bauxite and Gallium Mining Builds the Future
In a world racing toward AI, electric vehicles, and advanced defense systems, the minerals beneath our feet have never been more critical. Bauxite—the reddish-brown ore that becomes aluminum—and its often-overlooked companion gallium are powering the technologies of tomorrow. And right now, there are real opportunities for people ready to roll up their sleeves and work in the mines and refineries that extract them.

America’s Bauxite Heartland: Arkansas
The largest bauxite deposits in the United States sit in central Arkansas, spanning parts of Pulaski and Saline Counties near Little Rock and Benton. For decades, roughly 90% of all U.S. bauxite came from this region. While large-scale metallurgical mining has slowed, the geology remains, and smaller operations continue for abrasives, chemicals, and other uses. These deposits formed through intense weathering of nepheline syenite, leaving behind aluminum-rich material that still holds value.

Australia’s Gallium Moment
Australia leads the world in bauxite production. At Alcoa’s Wagerup alumina refinery in Western Australia, a major new project is turning that bauxite into something even more strategic: gallium. Backed by the Australian, U.S., and Japanese governments, the facility is set to produce about 100 tonnes per year—roughly 10% of global demand. Gallium is essential for semiconductors, LEDs, radar, and high-performance electronics. China currently dominates supply, so diversifying it creates both economic and security value.

Importantly, the gallium is recovered as a byproduct of the existing Bayer process used to make alumina. No brand-new mine is required for this particular plant, but it supports the broader bauxite mining and refining ecosystem that keeps the feedstock flowing. The build is expected to create up to 200 construction jobs and around 20 permanent roles once operating.

Why Work in These Mines and Refineries?
Mining and mineral processing offer strong wages, skills that transfer across industries, and a sense of purpose. You’re not just extracting rock—you’re enabling the phones, planes, cars, and defense systems people rely on. Roles range from equipment operators and heavy-vehicle drivers to process technicians, geologists, environmental specialists, and tradespeople. Training pathways exist, and many companies invest heavily in safety and career development.

Projects like the Wagerup gallium plant show how government and industry are aligning to grow the sector. With elevated prices for critical minerals and explicit policy support, the outlook for skilled workers is brighter than it has been in years. Whether in Arkansas’ historic districts or Australia’s modern operations, the need for people who can operate safely, solve problems, and keep production running is real.

The Bigger Picture
Bauxite becomes alumina, which becomes aluminum—the lightweight metal in everything from beverage cans to aircraft. Gallium, recovered along the way, underpins next-generation chips. Together they illustrate why domestic and allied production matters. For anyone considering a career change, a first job, or a move into the resources sector, the combination of practical work, competitive pay, and strategic importance makes mining a compelling choice.

If you’re ready to build something tangible that powers the future, look at the opportunities in bauxite and critical-mineral operations. The ground is ready. The question is whether you are.

  Last week was a rough one. The Dow slipped 0.9%, the S&P 500 lost 2.7% and the Nasdaq dropped 3.4%. Friday offered some relief, with the S&P up 0.3% and the Nasdaq up 1.1%, even though the Dow gave back 0.5%.  

𝘼 𝙅𝙤𝙗𝙨 𝙍𝙚𝙥𝙤𝙧𝙩 𝙏𝙝𝙖𝙩 𝘾𝙖𝙡𝙢𝙚𝙙 𝙉𝙚𝙧𝙫𝙚𝙨  

 October payrolls came in stronger than expected, and unemployment ticked down. That tells us the labor market isn't cracking, even with all the worry about AI replacing white-collar workers. It also raises the odds of a December Fed hike. Stocks shrugged that off, which I read as a good sign.  

𝙏𝙝𝙚 𝘼𝙄 𝙏𝙧𝙖𝙙𝙚 𝙄𝙨𝙣'𝙩 𝙊𝙫𝙚𝙧

  After the midterms, the question is what a tougher political backdrop means for AI spending. Several strategists point the same way: the buildout slows but doesn't stop.  
- Fears of data center moratoriums in places like Texas look overblown. Nothing so far changes the long-term outlook for construction. 
- A slower pace could actually help the big hyperscalers. They'd need to raise less outside money and could lean more on their own free cash flow. 
- More disciplined spending could even ease inflation pressure. That would help the Fed, because "bazooka-style" AI capex has been feeding the heat in the economy.  
Put simply, some of the AI anxiety in equities is taking away the worry that the AI boom would overheat the economy.  

𝙋𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙚𝙣𝙘𝙚 𝙄𝙨 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙋𝙡𝙖𝙮

  The demand for AI is still there. What's being debated is the timing of returns on all that invested cash, and whether a Democratic wave means stiffer regulation for a while. That's a timing question, not a verdict on the technology.  Two events could shape sentiment this month: Nvidia's earnings on November 17 and Anthropic's expected IPO ahead of Thanksgiving. Both will give the market fresh clues about where AI goes next.  

𝘾𝙡𝙤𝙨𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙏𝙝𝙤𝙪𝙜𝙝𝙩𝙨

  I wouldn't bail on AI because of one ugly week. I also wouldn't expect the explosive chip-stock gains we saw earlier this year to come back quickly. The more realistic path is slower, steadier growth with a broader group of leaders. That's one more reason to stay diversified and not lean too hard on any single theme.  

Happy Investing, 
Simion

text:
$STONK is now down 88% from ATH.

i'm going to stop with my bearish tweets now.

the token has reached a point where it offers a valid r/r for people who want to bet on an onchain comeback.

but there are definitely some learnings to take away here:

- annualizing revenue/buybacks is (mostly) a meme. it's a double edged sword, because at the same time it's the best reference point to determine fair token value. but it only makes sense if you're convinced the revenue is sustainable. otherwise, treat the narrative as a short-term trade.

- which brings us to point two. i already tweeted about this a few days ago, but checking whether products have a moat is very important. if you can answer that with yes, annualizing revenue becomes a lot more valid. launchpads on the other hand usually don't have one, and the past has shown that already.

- don't marry your bags. it's honestly easier said than done to have an unbiased opinion. but in general, if you're bullish on something, you should actively try to listen to the critical voices.

last but not least, i want to say that hindsight analysis is always easy.

we've seen some unexpected bearish events over the last few weeks that accelerated the downtrend.

there are definitely scenarios in which onchain would have had a comeback and STONK bulls would have been right.

Kimi Antonelli won Sunday’s Italian Grand Prix with team-mate George Russell P2.

It was a thrilling drive from Kimi as he charged through the field from P19 to become the first Italian to win their home race since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966.

It also marks Mercedes 250th Grand Prix victory as a power unit manufacturer and the marque’s eighth victory at Monza; it’s first since 2018 at the ‘Temple of Speed’.

Starting out of position, Kimi started on the Hard tyre but was able to change to the Medium compound under an early race red flag. By that point, he had already gained seven places to run P12.

George meanwhile ran the conventional one-stop from P2 by starting on the Medium and taking the Hard under the red flag, with the clear goal to run to the end on that tyre as he led.

Kimi’s progressed continued once the race restarted and cycled through to battle his team-mate for the lead.

A mid-race Virtual Safety Car gave the team the option of pitting Kimi for a new Medium tyre, with signs suggesting that his original Medium tyre wouldn’t have the life to get to the end of the race.

He rejoined in P6 but made short work of cars ahead; in the final stages he closed the gap to George before making the pass for the lead with three laps left.

Our duo took the flag comfortably ahead of the rest of the field to secure the win, and the 50th for an Italian in F1.

Deputy Technical Director Simone Resta represented the team on the podium at his home race.

The team now leads the Constructors’ Championship by 122 points with Kimi heading the Drivers’ standings by 66 points from his team-mate George.

What makes the Austrian Grand Prix special – and why you should see it

Discover what makes the F1 weekend in Austria unmissable.

The Austrian Grand Prix is a classic, and might just be held at one of the most picturesque track on the F1 calendar. Set in the Styrian hills, around 700m above sea level, the short track features rapid lap times and plenty of overtaking opportunities.

Despite the Red Bull Ring having the fewest corners of any circuit on the schedule, it's seen many unforgettable moments throughout the years – and, as the name might suggest, is the track that Red Bull calls home.

Let's take a look at just some of the reasons why Austria is so alluring.

Austrian racing heritage

Austria, despite it's relatively small population, has heaps of racing heritage. Triple World Champion Niki Lauda was born in Vienna, winning titles for Ferrari and McLaren, and was a major factor behind Mercedes’ success while helping convince Lewis Hamilton to join the outfit in 2013.

Jochen Rindt was Austria's first champion – the only posthumous F1 title winner, having tragically passed away during his dominant 1970 season. Gerhard Berger, while never taking the title himself, scored 10 wins during his illustrious career.

More recently, the late Austrian entrepreneur Dietrich Mateschitz and former Austrian F1 racer Helmut Marko – in his role as motorsport advisor – played key roles in Red Bull's success, with the team clinching eight Drivers’ and six Constructors’ titles.

When is the 2026 Austrian Grand Prix?

The 2026 Austrian Grand Prix weekend begins on Friday 26 June, with F1 cars hitting the track for the first two Free Practice sessions, before Free Practice 3 and Qualifying take place on Saturday 27 June. The Grand Prix itself is on Sunday 28 June, at 1500 local time.

What makes the Austrian Grand Prix special – and why you should see it

Discover what makes the F1 weekend in Austria unmissable.

The Austrian Grand Prix is a classic, and might just be held at one of the most picturesque track on the F1 calendar. Set in the Styrian hills, around 700m above sea level, the short track features rapid lap times and plenty of overtaking opportunities.

Despite the Red Bull Ring having the fewest corners of any circuit on the schedule, it's seen many unforgettable moments throughout the years – and, as the name might suggest, is the track that Red Bull calls home.

Let's take a look at just some of the reasons why Austria is so alluring.

Austrian racing heritage

Austria, despite it's relatively small population, has heaps of racing heritage. Triple World Champion Niki Lauda was born in Vienna, winning titles for Ferrari and McLaren, and was a major factor behind Mercedes’ success while helping convince Lewis Hamilton to join the outfit in 2013.

Jochen Rindt was Austria's first champion – the only posthumous F1 title winner, having tragically passed away during his dominant 1970 season. Gerhard Berger, while never taking the title himself, scored 10 wins during his illustrious career.

More recently, the late Austrian entrepreneur Dietrich Mateschitz and former Austrian F1 racer Helmut Marko – in his role as motorsport advisor – played key roles in Red Bull's success, with the team clinching eight Drivers’ and six Constructors’ titles.

When is the 2026 Austrian Grand Prix?

The 2026 Austrian Grand Prix weekend begins on Friday 26 June, with F1 cars hitting the track for the first two Free Practice sessions, before Free Practice 3 and Qualifying take place on Saturday 27 June. The Grand Prix itself is on Sunday 28 June, at 1500 local time.

Kimi Antonelli won Sunday’s Italian Grand Prix with team-mate George Russell P2.

It was a thrilling drive from Kimi as he charged through the field from P19 to become the first Italian to win their home race since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966.
It also marks Mercedes 250th Grand Prix victory as a power unit manufacturer and the marque’s eighth victory at Monza; it’s first since 2018 at the ‘Temple of Speed’.

Starting out of position, Kimi started on the Hard tyre but was able to change to the Medium compound under an early race red flag. By that point, he had already gained seven places to run P12.

George meanwhile ran the conventional one-stop from P2 by starting on the Medium and taking the Hard under the red flag, with the clear goal to run to the end on that tyre as he led.

Kimi’s progressed continued once the race restarted and cycled through to battle his team-mate for the lead.
A mid-race Virtual Safety Car gave the team the option of pitting Kimi for a new Medium tyre, with signs suggesting that his original Medium tyre wouldn’t have the life to get to the end of the race.

He rejoined in P6 but made short work of cars ahead; in the final stages he closed the gap to George before making the pass for the lead with three laps left.

Our duo took the flag comfortably ahead of the rest of the field to secure the win, and the 50th for an Italian in F1.

Deputy Technical Director Simone Resta represented the team on the podium at his home race.

The team now leads the Constructors’ Championship by 122 points with Kimi heading the Drivers’ standings by 66 points from his team-mate George.

George Russell claimed victory at the Austrian Grand Prix for his second win of 2026, holding off Max Verstappen by 1.6 seconds while teammate Kimi Antonelli took third for a Mercedes 1-3 finish. Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton locked out second and third in qualifying, but strategy and tire issues dropped them to eighth and fifth. The weekend's fun moment came from Hamilton and Leclerc's fan stage jokes about secret skydives, highlighting their budding partnership as Mercedes leads constructors with 302 points over Ferrari's 204.

What makes the Austrian Grand Prix special – and why you should see it

Discover what makes the F1 weekend in Austria unmissable.
The Austrian Grand Prix is a classic, and might just be held at one of the most picturesque track on the F1 calendar. Set in the Styrian hills, around 700m above sea level, the short track features rapid lap times and plenty of overtaking opportunities.
Despite the Red Bull Ring having the fewest corners of any circuit on the schedule, it's seen many unforgettable moments throughout the years – and, as the name might suggest, is the track that Red Bull calls home.

Let's take a look at just some of the reasons why Austria is so alluring.

Austrian racing heritage

Austria, despite it's relatively small population, has heaps of racing heritage. Triple World Champion Niki Lauda was born in Vienna, winning titles for Ferrari and McLaren, and was a major factor behind Mercedes’ success while helping convince Lewis Hamilton to join the outfit in 2013.

Jochen Rindt was Austria's first champion – the only posthumous F1 title winner, having tragically passed away during his dominant 1970 season. Gerhard Berger, while never taking the title himself, scored 10 wins during his illustrious career.

More recently, the late Austrian entrepreneur Dietrich Mateschitz and former Austrian F1 racer Helmut Marko – in his role as motorsport advisor – played key roles in Red Bull's success, with the team clinching eight Drivers’ and six Constructors’ titles.

When is the 2026 Austrian Grand Prix?

The 2026 Austrian Grand Prix weekend begins on Friday 26 June, with F1 cars hitting the track for the first two Free Practice sessions, before Free Practice 3 and Qualifying take place on Saturday 27 June. The Grand Prix itself is on Sunday 28 June, at 1500 local time.

Aegina Island – Just an Hour from Athens

An island escape doesn't always mean travelling far. Just off the coast of Attica, Aegina offers a refreshing change of scenery, with a picturesque harbour, traditional villages, beautiful beaches and a fascinating history waiting to be explored.

The island is perhaps best known for its pistachios, but there's much more to discover beyond its famous local produce. Aegina combines a relaxed seaside atmosphere with archaeological treasures, charming countryside and a coastline dotted with inviting swimming spots.

Start your visit in Aegina Town, where fishing boats and small yachts fill the harbour and the waterfront cafés provide the perfect place to watch island life unfold. Wander through the narrow streets, browse local shops and pick up some pistachios to take home.

There are plenty of experiences to add to your day:
•  Visit the Temple of Aphaia: One of Greece's most impressive ancient temples, beautifully positioned above the surrounding landscape.
•  Explore Aegina Town: Enjoy the harbour, traditional architecture, local shops and lively little squares.
•  Discover Perdika: A charming fishing village with waterfront tavernas and lovely views across the sea.
•  Find a favourite beach: Head towards Agia Marina, Marathonas or one of the island's smaller coastal spots for a swim.
•  Taste the local pistachios: Try fresh pistachios, sweets, pastries and other products made using the island's famous crop.

Aegina also has a quieter side. Take a drive through its interior, visit traditional settlements and enjoy the landscape of olive groves, pistachio trees and low hills.

Whether you visit for a day trip or decide to stay for a few nights, Aegina makes it easy to combine sightseeing, good food and time by the sea. It's one of those islands that proves you don't have to travel far from Athens to experience a very different pace of life.

text:
I’ve been fixated on this story over the weekend.

Taiwan detained Lin Te-wang, chairman of the Taiwan People’s Communist Party, over allegations that he accepted CCP funding and direction to contest the November 28 local elections. (Including offers to voters for free trips to mainland China!)

Why would China invest resources in such a… relatively insignificant and hyper-local contest?

If you’ve followed Chinese election interference in the past, you’ll get it. China doesn’t need an electoral victory to generate returns. 

This is purely soft power as constituency cultivation. Tiny, losing campaigns can establish personal relationships whose value can emerge years later. Option value!

Democracies often underestimate how local political influence can accumulate in networks that appear, at face value, to be inconsequential. Taiwan makes this more interesting with its history of political brokerage.

Individuals with little authority may nevertheless connect disparate groups and provide access to people considerably more powerful than themselves. (Sometimes we call this “structural holes.” You become valuable, as a broker, simply by existing as a bridge in the white space between disconnected social groups.)

These grassroots networks provide insight into social grievances, which then create opportunities to cultivate figures whose institutional access evolves over time. 

Taiwan’s Mazu temple networks offer a solid precedent.

This also allows an actor to battle-test narratives and understand which messages resonate in targeted communities before attempting a broader influence campaign. There is a screening function here. 

But there are limits to this approach! It’s actually really hard to “purchase” (per se) loyalty. We have to remember that these networks are human and still have agency. Intermediaries are self-interested and financing spoiler candidates have diminishing returns over successive cycles.

Foot-in-the-door effect. (There’s a recent study of this phenomenon in Kinmen, where China’s united front possibly produced resistance.)

The principal-agent dilemma cuts both ways.

The counterintelligence mission then poses a direct threat to democratic legitimacy, as distinguishing foreign financing and direction from lawful association and free speech risks mistaking ideological sympathy for control, especially when these relationships develop slowly over long periods of time.

There’s an attribution problem too. Back in September, Taiwan upheld an acquittal of a person accused of facilitating election interference via subsidized travel to China, based on insufficient evidence.

Are Taiwan and its partners equipped to handle this small-scale, incremental, multi-cycle approach to cultivation and influence? I’m not sure. 

It requires an attention to detail and level of foresight that looks far beyond each election cycle, into benign relationships and networks that won’t be consequential for years, and I’m worried we’re barely able to get a handle on the present.

text:
2/2: Talisman’s powers, training and limits

The tattoos in Part 1 give Talisman weapons and creatures he can call on when he needs them. Those summons can also save people: in Prophecy, two luminous canine-shaped creatures push dockworkers clear of falling containers.

The wolf pack and pair of birds also show that he can keep several creatures active at once. His power reaches further than those summons, though.

Energy attacks

Talisman fires magic from his eyes and hands. Beyond the Day of the Dead eye attacks covered in Part 1, he uses them against Olgar in Tarot and the orc Karn in Prophecy.

Tarot also shows him firing from his hands, knocking Cynder back with a fist-directed blast and releasing a wider burst that drives the Queen of Swords and nearby soldiers away. During the later fight, energy streams from both eyes. Day of the Dead #5 also shows his bindings breaking amid golden magic as he brings out a sword and fires an eye blast at the undead around him.

These attacks vary in color and size. The comics never put a dependable number on their range or damage, and a different color does not automatically make a blast a new power.

Fire

The burning neck tattoo is one example. He also relights a fallen lantern with a hand gesture in Day of the Dead #4. That gives him a quieter, practical use for fire alongside the close-range defensive burst.

Those are the fire abilities actually shown. They do not establish unlimited control over flames.

Sight and sensing magic

His origin account says the tattoos let him see into other spectrums. In the swamp, his markings glow as he recognizes the dark power around him.

He can perceive things beyond ordinary sight and sense magic, although the books do not explain the full range of either ability or connect them to one specific tattoo.

He also speaks with Mama Cal’s manifested ghost in Prophecy. The large undead attacks in that story belong to Mystere.

Combining power with someone else

In Tarot, Talisman and Shimmer join hands and channel energy together. This follows the discussion of using the same energy he accessed in the temple.

The clearest light-powered transformation comes with Mystere in Myths & Legends Quarterly: Prophecy (https://t.co/kJYHkjUFUk). Following Mama Cal’s guidance, they join hands and bring out the light inside them. His tattoos turn white, armor forms around them, and he takes up a sword and shield.

Together they break apart Damien’s shadow manifestation. Damien himself survives.

This state does not last. Both characters feel the light fading afterward. They found a way to reach it together, but Prophecy does not leave Talisman permanently free of the darkness or show him entering that state whenever he wants on his own.

Armor, fighting skill and endurance

Talisman wears armor as the King of Pentacles, and Prophecy shows armor forming during the joint light transformation. It offers protection, but he can still be restrained. Mystere has to help free him from the shadow creature’s tendrils.

He also knows how to fight without magic. He was taught to defend himself, and Tarot shows him training with the Order of Light. He uses swords in close combat, practices hand-to-hand fighting and keeps fighting while directing his powers.

He can take a serious beating, too. Judgment kicks him through a masonry wall in Day of the Dead, and he keeps going despite the pain. Mystere leaves him bloodied in Prophecy, but he gets back up.

He still gets hurt. Those scenes do not establish invulnerability, a healing factor or a precise superhuman strength rating.

The cost

His mother could fade the tattoos, but using their dark magic makes them darker and more permanent. Every use risks pulling him further toward the role the Order chose for him.

There are practical limits as well. After sending wolves to occupy his enemies, he admits he does not know how long the spell will last. Judgment puts him to sleep with a spell. He can be overwhelmed, captured or restrained, and training does not immediately give him control over everything he can do.

Talisman has weapons, creatures, ranged attacks, fire and unusual perception to draw on, with another route to power when he works with an ally. Saving someone can mean reaching for the very magic he is trying to escape. That problem stays with him even when the immediate fight is over.

text:
His name is Wade Wilson. Same as Deadpool. He was sentenced to death the same summer Deadpool & Wolverine hit theaters.

On October 7, 2019, in Cape Coral, Florida, he killed two women he had never met. Kristine Melton, 35, was strangled in her bed after a night out. Hours later he offered Diane Ruiz, 43, a ride while she walked to work. She hadn't missed a shift in five years. He choked her and ran her over.

That same morning a camera filmed him walk into a small business shirtless, barefoot and covered in blood, telling the owner he had killed someone. Then he called his father and confessed again. His father turned him in and later testified that his son sounded excited.

Asked why, he told detectives: "I just wanted to do it."

Before trial he got permission to wear makeup over his face tattoos. He never used it. Women wrote him love letters. The jury voted 9 to 3 and 10 to 2 for death. Before 2023, Florida needed all 12, which means under the old law he gets life.

After the sentence, his lawyers asked for one thing: send him to death row as soon as possible.

Did Florida get justice right, or just make it easier to kill a man when 3 of 12 people aren't sure?

US President Donald Trump has clarified that his offer to appoint UFC President and CEO Dana White as White House press secretary was a joke. Speaking to reporters in Florida on Sunday, November 8, Trump said he was "only kidding" when he announced the proposed appointment on social media a day earlier.

The 80-year-old president described the announcement as "just a little fun" and said he believed White liked the idea. Trump pointed to the six UFC fighters he had named as potential assistants, saying their inclusion should have made the joke obvious.

The 57-year-old White is a longtime friend and political supporter of Trump, having publicly backed his presidential campaigns. He also helped organise the UFC Freedom 250 event on the White House lawn in June 2026, marking America's 250th anniversary.
